tags.chapter_name: Center of Mass Momentum and Collision

question.text: An isolated particle of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>m</mi></math> is moving in the horizontal plane <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> along the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math>-axis, at a certain height above the ground. It suddenly explodes into two fragments of masses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>. An instant later, the smaller fragment is at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math>. The larger fragment at this instant is at

solution.text:
Before the explosion, the particle was moving along x-axis i.e., it has no y-component of velocity. Therefore, the centre of mass will not move in y-direction or we can say ycm=0.

Now,     ycm=m1y1+m2y2m1+m2

Therefore,      0=m/4+15+3m/4ym/4+3m/4

or,    y=-5 cm
